medical.title: Aging blocks the retina's ability to regrow lost neurons, a first-of-its-kind study finds
medical.summary: A new study from the laboratory of Levi Todd, Ph.D., at Upstate Medical University has found that aging significantly limits the ability of support cells in the retina, called glia, to be reprogrammed into new neurons, a finding with important implications for the future of regenerative medicine for age-related neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and glaucoma.

medical.title: Putting a price on preventive care: How Medicaid compares to other insurers in Virginia
medical.summary: Medicaid has a reputation for paying doctors less than other health insurers. But exactly how much less has been difficult to establish, particularly for the vast majority of Medicaid patients whose care is provided through private health plans.

medical.title: Tumor biology could guide mantle cell lymphoma treatment from the time of diagnosis
medical.summary: Today, treatment decisions for patients with mantle cell lymphoma are heavily based on age alone, although the disease can range from slow-growing (indolent) to very aggressive. In a new journal article, Ingrid Glimelius and co-authors suggest that it is time to let the disease's biology also guide treatment—and provide more effective interventions earlier for those at the highest risk of aggressive disease, while avoiding unnecessarily intensive treatment for patients with indolent disease.

medical.title: Testosterone maxxing is all the rage—but when it comes to fatherhood, less might be more
medical.summary: Testosterone is having a moment. On social media, it's being lauded for everything from building muscle to gaining wealth and sexual dominance.

medical.title: Experimental brain implants are on the rise. What happens after the trials are over?
medical.summary: In 2024, Elon Musk's Neuralink put its first brain implant into a human amid doubt from scientists and allegations of animal cruelty.

medical.title: AI models show promising results in ICU mortality predictions
medical.summary: Predicting mortality risk in intensive care unit (ICU) patients is a crucial part of medical treatment, and recent research has found artificial intelligence could help clinicians make more efficient and accurate decisions.

medical.title: Local neural wiring may set the brain's range of activity patterns
medical.summary: The human brain contains billions of neurons, specialized nerve cells that receive, transmit and process information through electrical and chemical signals. Human thoughts, sensory perceptions and behaviors are known to emerge not from the activity of individual neurons but from collective patterns of activity distributed across different neuron populations.

medical.title: The workout recovery techniques backed by science—and the ones that are just hype
medical.summary: Finishing a tough workout always feels good. That is, until a few hours later, when those uncomfortable muscle aches start setting in. This discomfort can linger for days—making easy, everyday tasks a challenge.

medical.title: Systems-level approaches crucial to translating research into aged care practice
medical.summary: Research continues to improve knowledge and understanding, but translating this research into clinical practice remains a challenge.

medical.title: Stanford scientists discover a seafood that can reverse signs of aging
medical.summary: A substance found in edible sea squirts appeared to reverse several signs of aging in older mice. Plasmalogen supplements improved memory and learning, strengthened connections between brain cells, reduced inflammation, and even helped the mice grow thicker, darker hair. Researchers believe the compounds may encourage brain regeneration and protect aging synapses.

medical.title: Break a sweat, hear more? Early results point to a surprising link between fitness and speech perception
medical.summary: It's easy to take hearing for granted.

medical.title: FDA approves first-in-class drug for polycythemia vera
medical.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Takeda Pharmaceuticals' Mimrylo (rusfertide) as a new treatment for adults with polycythemia vera who have not achieved adequate control with existing therapies.

medical.title: Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
medical.summary: UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. Those signals can alter which types of neurons are produced, including upper-layer neurons that are especially prominent in humans.

medical.title: New injectable treatment helps the brain rebuild after stroke
medical.summary: Duke researchers developed an injectable scaffold that helped stroke-damaged brains grow new blood vessels, support nerve regrowth, and recover movement in mice. The treatment appears to work partly by recruiting the body’s own immune cells, including neutrophils that may switch from damaging to helpful under the right conditions.

science.title: Shoppers buying online while drunk is big business—but who is responsible?
science.summary: One Sunday morning, Juliet* woke up to a delivery driver with a large package that she had no recollection of ordering. She was quick to dismiss it as an e-commerce mistake before the card inside helped solve the mystery: "To Sober Juliet, from your friend, Drunk Juliet."

science.title: Not a cheetah: Ancient DNA reveals the surprising Arctic life of extinct North American cat
science.summary: A new study led by researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz, has overturned decades of assumptions about Miracinonyx trumani, the extinct predator popularly known as the American cheetah. By analyzing nuclear paleogenomes and stable isotopes from fossils found as far north as the Yukon, scientists have discovered that this iconic cat was not a true cheetah but a highly adaptable relative of the puma that specialized in eating fish to survive in the Arctic.

science.title: Most money laundering arrests involve people under the age of 30
science.summary: The majority of money laundering arrests involve people under 30, a new analysis has found.

science.title: Rescue satellite gets close to NASA's doomed telescope, even if it can't save it
science.summary: A private spacecraft that was supposed to supply a lifeline to NASA's Swift Observatory managed to get close to the sinking telescope and even snap photos more than a week after the rescue was abandoned.

science.title: Divergent molecular mechanisms for fungal plant biomass conversion
science.summary: Fungi are major degraders of plant biomass, including leaves, stems and roots. Investigating the molecular mechanisms that control this process is essential for identifying ways to degrade and use lignocellulose, a recalcitrant waste-product residue from biofeedstocks and agricultural residues, and accelerate the development of biotechnology. It is also essential for deepening understanding of the ecological role of fungi in the global carbon cycle.

science.title: Critically endangered pygmy raccoons observed making their own paper toys
science.summary: Some of the most intriguing scientific breakthroughs happen when researchers aren't explicitly looking for them. Take, for example, the pygmy raccoon (Procyon pygmaeus), a critically endangered species that lives only on Cozumel Island, Mexico. Scientists were observing them for a study on the impact of tourism on their populations when they made an accidental discovery.

science.title: An activity-based probe library for identifying protein function
science.summary: Proteins are vital to living systems. They build and repair tissues, act as enzymes to speed chemical reactions, regulate hormones and transport nutrients—all of which are important for developing next-generation bioproducts and advancing bioengineering and biotechnology.

science.title: Brainless sea sponges use sunset to prepare for metamorphosis—and attach in 30 minutes
science.summary: Well before I start collecting coats, keys or shoes, my dog always knows when we're about to leave. By picking up on subtle cues, he anticipates our next movements, reminding me he's smarter than he often shows. But anticipation isn't always about brains. Our new research reveals that even an animal with no brain at all can anticipate what's coming next.

science.title: Lunar Occultation of Venus
science.summary: On Wednesday, June 17, skywatchers across the United States—and parts of Canada—enjoyed a rare event: a daytime lunar occultation of Venus. A lunar occultation occurs when the Moon moves directly in front of another celestial object from our viewpoint on Earth, briefly hiding it from sight. This time, the Moon slipped in front of Venus […]

science.title: Davyne changes color beyond human sight, opening path to invisible security tags
science.summary: While studying the properties of hackmanite, researchers created a new material called davyne that changes color in the near-infrared region. The color change cannot be detected with the human eye, but only with a spectrometer or an infrared-sensitive camera. The researchers studied what caused the color change and tested the material's possible applications, for example, as an invisible anti-counterfeit tag.

science.title: AI-driven polymer discovery could replace years of trial and error with closed-loop testing
science.summary: In the realm of materials science, there is a plethora of datasets and tools at our disposal—the issue is how to effectively use these resources in harmony. Researchers at the Advanced Institute for Materials Research (WPI-AIMR), Tohoku University, have identified major bottlenecks holding back artificial intelligence-driven polymer innovation and created a system that integrates multiple tools (such as polymer databases, predictive models, AI agents and automated laboratories).

science.title: AI helps dentists practice the conversations that matter
science.summary: A University of Rochester collaboration is using an AI-powered virtual patient to help dentists strengthen their communication, build trust and better respond to patients' fears and concerns. For many patients, sitting in a dental chair can be stressful long before treatment begins.

science.title: Venice Lagoon provides living laboratory for researchers studying climate change
science.summary: Venice really is sinking. Sort of. The home of gondolas, bridges and canals is built across a collection of islands, and the sediments beneath them are gradually compacting, causing the ground to subside. But while the land moves down, climate change is pushing the water up—making the shallow lagoon surrounding the Italian city an increasingly vulnerable environment.

science.title: Can a full moon really bring bad luck? What about Friday the 13th?
science.summary: Jeffrey Rosenthal was a young professor at the University of Toronto when he discovered he was born on a Friday—though not just any Friday.

science.title: Wrinkled carbon nitride challenges flat-sheet model for photocatalyst design
science.summary: Graphene is flat. But that doesn't mean other 2D materials—particularly those containing more than one element—necessarily share the same structure. In the past, researchers have often simplified these materials by modeling them as perfectly flat sheets.

science.title: How damaged teeth can reinforce stigma and disadvantage
science.summary: For women involved in street sex work who took part in our research, damaged or missing teeth were more than a health problem. They could become visible reminders of lives they were trying to change.

science.title: How hibernating squirrels retain sense of touch in the cold
science.summary: For most mammals, cold suppresses neural activity and diminishes the sense of touch. But the thirteen-lined ground squirrel can detect touch in conditions as low as 4°C (39°F), about as cold as the inside of a refrigerator, finds a new Yale study published in Current Biology.

science.title: Prom season can increase body image anxiety for some teens—how parents can help
science.summary: Prom is one of the most exciting events on the school calendar for many high school seniors.

science.title: Orange hydrogen: Could Western Australia's rocks help power a low-carbon future?
science.summary: Deep beneath parts of Western Australia, injecting CO2-rich water into iron-rich rocks may offer an unexpected opportunity for both clean energy production and carbon storage.

science.title: Iron Age Botswana site sourced copper across southern Africa—but tin from just one place
science.summary: Around 700 years ago, people living on hilltop settlements on the edge of the Kalahari wore beads, bangles and clips made from metal traded across the southern half of the African continent.

science.title: MIT turns bacteria into living transistors
science.summary: MIT researchers have created bacterial “transistors” that can be wired together into living circuits capable of performing calculations and directing chemical signals. One day, these biological computers could coat plant roots or leaves, detecting environmental threats and automatically triggering defenses.

science.title: Dying radio galaxies fade faster than scientists expected
science.summary: Astronomers have identified a surprisingly young population of fading radio galaxies whose supermassive black holes have already switched off their powerful jets. The confirmed remnants range from about 8 to 42 million years old, suggesting many may disappear from view much faster than previously recognized. More distant remnants also seem to fade especially quickly, helping explain why they have been so difficult to detect.

science.title: Dark matter detector finds a strange signal scientists can’t yet explain
science.summary: The LUX-ZEPLIN experiment has detected a rare particle interaction that looks unusually difficult to explain as ordinary background noise and appeared where dark matter might be expected. Scientists are not claiming a discovery yet, but additional data could show whether this single mysterious event is the first hint of a long-sought dark matter particle.

science.title: Scientists discover a bizarre “devil flower” hidden in Thailand
science.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange black “devil flower” in Thailand that lives mostly underground, steals nutrients from fungi, and looks strikingly unlike a typical plant. The newly named Thismia daemona is known from fewer than 50 individuals and may already be critically endangered.

environment.title: Superb fairywrens disappearing in Australia’s capital: Conserving insects could help save them
environment.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

environment.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
environment.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

environment.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
environment.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

environment.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

environment.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

mix_items.title: Aging blocks the retina's ability to regrow lost neurons, a first-of-its-kind study finds
mix_items.summary: A new study from the laboratory of Levi Todd, Ph.D., at Upstate Medical University has found that aging significantly limits the ability of support cells in the retina, called glia, to be reprogrammed into new neurons, a finding with important implications for the future of regenerative medicine for age-related neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and glaucoma.

mix_items.summary: One Sunday morning, Juliet* woke up to a delivery driver with a large package that she had no recollection of ordering. She was quick to dismiss it as an e-commerce mistake before the card inside helped solve the mystery: "To Sober Juliet, from your friend, Drunk Juliet."

mix_items.title: Not a cheetah: Ancient DNA reveals the surprising Arctic life of extinct North American cat
mix_items.summary: A new study led by researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz, has overturned decades of assumptions about Miracinonyx trumani, the extinct predator popularly known as the American cheetah. By analyzing nuclear paleogenomes and stable isotopes from fossils found as far north as the Yukon, scientists have discovered that this iconic cat was not a true cheetah but a highly adaptable relative of the puma that specialized in eating fish to survive in the Arctic.

mix_items.title: Putting a price on preventive care: How Medicaid compares to other insurers in Virginia
mix_items.summary: Medicaid has a reputation for paying doctors less than other health insurers. But exactly how much less has been difficult to establish, particularly for the vast majority of Medicaid patients whose care is provided through private health plans.

mix_items.title: Most money laundering arrests involve people under the age of 30
mix_items.summary: The majority of money laundering arrests involve people under 30, a new analysis has found.

mix_items.title: Rescue satellite gets close to NASA's doomed telescope, even if it can't save it
mix_items.summary: A private spacecraft that was supposed to supply a lifeline to NASA's Swift Observatory managed to get close to the sinking telescope and even snap photos more than a week after the rescue was abandoned.

mix_items.title: Tumor biology could guide mantle cell lymphoma treatment from the time of diagnosis
mix_items.summary: Today, treatment decisions for patients with mantle cell lymphoma are heavily based on age alone, although the disease can range from slow-growing (indolent) to very aggressive. In a new journal article, Ingrid Glimelius and co-authors suggest that it is time to let the disease's biology also guide treatment—and provide more effective interventions earlier for those at the highest risk of aggressive disease, while avoiding unnecessarily intensive treatment for patients with indolent disease.

mix_items.title: Divergent molecular mechanisms for fungal plant biomass conversion
mix_items.summary: Fungi are major degraders of plant biomass, including leaves, stems and roots. Investigating the molecular mechanisms that control this process is essential for identifying ways to degrade and use lignocellulose, a recalcitrant waste-product residue from biofeedstocks and agricultural residues, and accelerate the development of biotechnology. It is also essential for deepening understanding of the ecological role of fungi in the global carbon cycle.

mix_items.title: Critically endangered pygmy raccoons observed making their own paper toys
mix_items.summary: Some of the most intriguing scientific breakthroughs happen when researchers aren't explicitly looking for them. Take, for example, the pygmy raccoon (Procyon pygmaeus), a critically endangered species that lives only on Cozumel Island, Mexico. Scientists were observing them for a study on the impact of tourism on their populations when they made an accidental discovery.

mix_items.title: An activity-based probe library for identifying protein function
mix_items.summary: Proteins are vital to living systems. They build and repair tissues, act as enzymes to speed chemical reactions, regulate hormones and transport nutrients—all of which are important for developing next-generation bioproducts and advancing bioengineering and biotechnology.

mix_items.title: Brainless sea sponges use sunset to prepare for metamorphosis—and attach in 30 minutes
mix_items.summary: Well before I start collecting coats, keys or shoes, my dog always knows when we're about to leave. By picking up on subtle cues, he anticipates our next movements, reminding me he's smarter than he often shows. But anticipation isn't always about brains. Our new research reveals that even an animal with no brain at all can anticipate what's coming next.

mix_items.title: Lunar Occultation of Venus
mix_items.summary: On Wednesday, June 17, skywatchers across the United States—and parts of Canada—enjoyed a rare event: a daytime lunar occultation of Venus. A lunar occultation occurs when the Moon moves directly in front of another celestial object from our viewpoint on Earth, briefly hiding it from sight. This time, the Moon slipped in front of Venus […]

mix_items.title: Davyne changes color beyond human sight, opening path to invisible security tags
mix_items.summary: While studying the properties of hackmanite, researchers created a new material called davyne that changes color in the near-infrared region. The color change cannot be detected with the human eye, but only with a spectrometer or an infrared-sensitive camera. The researchers studied what caused the color change and tested the material's possible applications, for example, as an invisible anti-counterfeit tag.

mix_items.title: Testosterone maxxing is all the rage—but when it comes to fatherhood, less might be more
mix_items.summary: Testosterone is having a moment. On social media, it's being lauded for everything from building muscle to gaining wealth and sexual dominance.

mix_items.title: Experimental brain implants are on the rise. What happens after the trials are over?
mix_items.summary: In 2024, Elon Musk's Neuralink put its first brain implant into a human amid doubt from scientists and allegations of animal cruelty.

mix_items.title: AI-driven polymer discovery could replace years of trial and error with closed-loop testing
mix_items.summary: In the realm of materials science, there is a plethora of datasets and tools at our disposal—the issue is how to effectively use these resources in harmony. Researchers at the Advanced Institute for Materials Research (WPI-AIMR), Tohoku University, have identified major bottlenecks holding back artificial intelligence-driven polymer innovation and created a system that integrates multiple tools (such as polymer databases, predictive models, AI agents and automated laboratories).

mix_items.title: AI helps dentists practice the conversations that matter
mix_items.summary: A University of Rochester collaboration is using an AI-powered virtual patient to help dentists strengthen their communication, build trust and better respond to patients' fears and concerns. For many patients, sitting in a dental chair can be stressful long before treatment begins.

mix_items.title: Venice Lagoon provides living laboratory for researchers studying climate change
mix_items.summary: Venice really is sinking. Sort of. The home of gondolas, bridges and canals is built across a collection of islands, and the sediments beneath them are gradually compacting, causing the ground to subside. But while the land moves down, climate change is pushing the water up—making the shallow lagoon surrounding the Italian city an increasingly vulnerable environment.

mix_items.title: Can a full moon really bring bad luck? What about Friday the 13th?
mix_items.summary: Jeffrey Rosenthal was a young professor at the University of Toronto when he discovered he was born on a Friday—though not just any Friday.

mix_items.title: AI models show promising results in ICU mortality predictions
mix_items.summary: Predicting mortality risk in intensive care unit (ICU) patients is a crucial part of medical treatment, and recent research has found artificial intelligence could help clinicians make more efficient and accurate decisions.

mix_items.title: Local neural wiring may set the brain's range of activity patterns
mix_items.summary: The human brain contains billions of neurons, specialized nerve cells that receive, transmit and process information through electrical and chemical signals. Human thoughts, sensory perceptions and behaviors are known to emerge not from the activity of individual neurons but from collective patterns of activity distributed across different neuron populations.

mix_items.title: Wrinkled carbon nitride challenges flat-sheet model for photocatalyst design
mix_items.summary: Graphene is flat. But that doesn't mean other 2D materials—particularly those containing more than one element—necessarily share the same structure. In the past, researchers have often simplified these materials by modeling them as perfectly flat sheets.

mix_items.title: The workout recovery techniques backed by science—and the ones that are just hype
mix_items.summary: Finishing a tough workout always feels good. That is, until a few hours later, when those uncomfortable muscle aches start setting in. This discomfort can linger for days—making easy, everyday tasks a challenge.

mix_items.title: How damaged teeth can reinforce stigma and disadvantage
mix_items.summary: For women involved in street sex work who took part in our research, damaged or missing teeth were more than a health problem. They could become visible reminders of lives they were trying to change.

mix_items.title: Systems-level approaches crucial to translating research into aged care practice
mix_items.summary: Research continues to improve knowledge and understanding, but translating this research into clinical practice remains a challenge.

mix_items.title: How hibernating squirrels retain sense of touch in the cold
mix_items.summary: For most mammals, cold suppresses neural activity and diminishes the sense of touch. But the thirteen-lined ground squirrel can detect touch in conditions as low as 4°C (39°F), about as cold as the inside of a refrigerator, finds a new Yale study published in Current Biology.

mix_items.title: Stanford scientists discover a seafood that can reverse signs of aging
mix_items.summary: A substance found in edible sea squirts appeared to reverse several signs of aging in older mice. Plasmalogen supplements improved memory and learning, strengthened connections between brain cells, reduced inflammation, and even helped the mice grow thicker, darker hair. Researchers believe the compounds may encourage brain regeneration and protect aging synapses.

mix_items.title: Prom season can increase body image anxiety for some teens—how parents can help
mix_items.summary: Prom is one of the most exciting events on the school calendar for many high school seniors.

mix_items.title: Break a sweat, hear more? Early results point to a surprising link between fitness and speech perception
mix_items.summary: It's easy to take hearing for granted.

mix_items.title: Orange hydrogen: Could Western Australia's rocks help power a low-carbon future?
mix_items.summary: Deep beneath parts of Western Australia, injecting CO2-rich water into iron-rich rocks may offer an unexpected opportunity for both clean energy production and carbon storage.

mix_items.title: Iron Age Botswana site sourced copper across southern Africa—but tin from just one place
mix_items.summary: Around 700 years ago, people living on hilltop settlements on the edge of the Kalahari wore beads, bangles and clips made from metal traded across the southern half of the African continent.

mix_items.title: FDA approves first-in-class drug for polycythemia vera
mix_items.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Takeda Pharmaceuticals' Mimrylo (rusfertide) as a new treatment for adults with polycythemia vera who have not achieved adequate control with existing therapies.

mix_items.title: MIT turns bacteria into living transistors
mix_items.summary: MIT researchers have created bacterial “transistors” that can be wired together into living circuits capable of performing calculations and directing chemical signals. One day, these biological computers could coat plant roots or leaves, detecting environmental threats and automatically triggering defenses.

mix_items.title: Dying radio galaxies fade faster than scientists expected
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have identified a surprisingly young population of fading radio galaxies whose supermassive black holes have already switched off their powerful jets. The confirmed remnants range from about 8 to 42 million years old, suggesting many may disappear from view much faster than previously recognized. More distant remnants also seem to fade especially quickly, helping explain why they have been so difficult to detect.

mix_items.title: Dark matter detector finds a strange signal scientists can’t yet explain
mix_items.summary: The LUX-ZEPLIN experiment has detected a rare particle interaction that looks unusually difficult to explain as ordinary background noise and appeared where dark matter might be expected. Scientists are not claiming a discovery yet, but additional data could show whether this single mysterious event is the first hint of a long-sought dark matter particle.

mix_items.title: Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
mix_items.summary: UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. Those signals can alter which types of neurons are produced, including upper-layer neurons that are especially prominent in humans.

mix_items.title: New injectable treatment helps the brain rebuild after stroke
mix_items.summary: Duke researchers developed an injectable scaffold that helped stroke-damaged brains grow new blood vessels, support nerve regrowth, and recover movement in mice. The treatment appears to work partly by recruiting the body’s own immune cells, including neutrophils that may switch from damaging to helpful under the right conditions.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a bizarre “devil flower” hidden in Thailand
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange black “devil flower” in Thailand that lives mostly underground, steals nutrients from fungi, and looks strikingly unlike a typical plant. The newly named Thismia daemona is known from fewer than 50 individuals and may already be critically endangered.

mix_items.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

mix_items.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga
mix_items.summary: CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

mix_items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
mix_items.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

mix_items.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
mix_items.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

mix_items.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

mix_items.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

satire_ro.title: Trump a schimbat numele Coca Cola în American Cola și acum trebuie să dea 500 de miliarde de dolari fraților Micula
